who_tobacco.title: Tobacco and nicotine
quotes: Tobacco kills more than 7 million people each year, including over 1.6 million non-smokers who are exposed to second-hand smoke.

Overview The tobacco epidemic is one of the biggest public health threats the world has ever faced, responsible for over 7 million deaths annually as well as disability and long-term suffering from tobacco-related diseases (1) .
More on monitoring tobacco use Global and country-level tobacco use prevalence trends and SDG 3.a.1 monitoring Second-hand smoke kills There is no safe level of exposure to second-hand tobacco smoke.
Second-hand smoke causes serious cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, including coronary heart disease and lung cancer, and kills more than 1.6 million people prematurely every year (1) .

who_tax.title: Raising taxes on tobacco
quotes: Evidence shows that significantly increasing tobacco excise taxes and prices is the single most effective and cost-effective measure for reducing tobacco use.
Raising taxes on tobacco products which lead to increases in their price makes tobacco less affordable.
Because youth and low-income groups are more responsive to increases in tobacco prices , they disproportionately enjoy the health and economic benefits of quitting and not starting.
Saving lives with tobacco taxes lessens the enormous healthcare burden and economic losses that result from tobacco-related disease.

nhs_pregnancy.title: Stop smoking in pregnancy - NHS
quotes: Every cigarette you smoke contains over 4,000 chemicals, many of which are dangerous, so smoking when you are pregnant harms your unborn baby.
Cigarettes can restrict the essential oxygen supply to your baby.
Benefits of stopping smoking in pregnancy Stopping smoking will help both you and your baby immediately.

For example, they are more likely to have problems keeping warm and are more likely to get infections you will reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) , also known as "cot death" Stopping smoking now will also help your baby later in life.

ucl_news_quit.title: Women in middle age less likely to quit smoking successfully | UCL News
quotes: The researchers found that: Middle aged women, aged 45 to 60, had the lowest quit success (18.1%) compared with younger (22.3%) and older women (20.6%) The lowest quit success was observed among middle-aged women from more deprived backgrounds (15.8% vs.
“Women in mid-life often face a combination of pressures that can make quitting smoking particularly challenging.
Women from more disadvantaged backgrounds are also more likely to have higher levels of nicotine dependence, which can make quitting harder.
“We need to better understand women’s experiences to ensure that stop smoking services are tailored to meet their specific needs.
